name: Republic of the Congo
summary: The former French Congo, independent in 1960, a Marxist state (1969–91), rich in oil; not to be confused with its larger neighbour, the DR Congo.

knownFor.label: Brazzaville and Kinshasa
knownFor.note: The two closest capitals in the world, across the Congo River.

location.value: Central Africa, west of the Congo River; about 342,000 km².

terrain.value: A coastal plain around Pointe-Noire, the Mayombe hills, the Batéké plateaus in the centre, and swampy rainforest in the north along the Congo and Ubangi rivers.

climate.value: Tropical: hot and humid all year with long rainy seasons; the equator crosses the north of the country.

resources.value: Offshore oil and gas, tropical timber, potash and iron ore, and large forests in the Congo Basin.

disasters.value: Seasonal floods along the Congo and Ubangi rivers; in March 2012 an arms depot explosion in Brazzaville killed hundreds of people.

population.value: About 6 million in the mid-2020s, with a very young population; most live in the south, especially in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire.

urbanisation.value: Highly urban for Africa: about two-thirds live in towns, mostly Brazzaville and the port of Pointe-Noire.

disease.value: Malaria is the main killer; HIV, tuberculosis and Ebola outbreaks in the north (2001–05) have also caused deaths.

migration.value: The civil wars of 1993–99 displaced hundreds of thousands; it has also hosted refugees from the DR Congo and Central African Republic.

economicBase.value: Oil from offshore fields near Pointe-Noire provides most export earnings and state revenue; timber and farming support many people.

tradeRoutes.value: The deep-water port of Pointe-Noire, linked to Brazzaville by the Congo–Océan Railway, and river transport on the Congo and Ubangi.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country with oil wealth, but many people live in poverty and public debt has been high.

moneyAndTax.value: The Central African CFA franc, pegged to the euro.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic; it was a one-party Marxist–Leninist state (1969–91) before multiparty politics returned in the 1990s.

keyRulers.value: Fulbert Youlou. Marien Ngouabi. Denis Sassou Nguesso.

succession.value: Sassou Nguesso has ruled most years since 1979.

institutions.value: A president, a two-chamber parliament and courts under the 2015 constitution; a National Conference in 1991 restored multiparty politics.

stability.value: Several coups after independence and civil wars in 1993–94 and 1997–99, which caused heavy loss of life in Brazzaville.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Congolese Armed Forces (army, navy and air force), which have played a major role in coups and in the civil wars.

majorWars.value: Civil wars of 1993–94 and 1997–99 between militias of rival politicians, including the Cobras, Ninjas and Cocoyes.

territoryChange.value: No change since 1960; its borders follow those of the colony of Middle Congo in French Equatorial Africa.

alliancesRivals.value: Close to France, and to the Soviet bloc in 1969–91; a member of the African Union and the CEMAC monetary union; China is a major partner.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville (founded 1971) is the main university; schools teach in French.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

religion.value: Mostly Christian, Catholic and Protestant, plus independent and revival churches; some people keep traditional beliefs.

languageWriting.value: French is official; Lingala and Kituba (Munukutuba) are national languages, alongside many local languages.

artsArchitecture.value: The Poto-Poto school of painting (founded 1951), the Sapeurs’ elegant fashion, Congolese rumba and Brazzaville’s Basilica of Sainte-Anne.

socialStructure.value: Many ethnic groups: Kongo peoples (the largest) in the south, Teke in the centre, Mbochi in the north, and Aka forest peoples.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity shaped by French, Lingala music and Brazzaville, alongside strong ethnic and regional loyalties.

dailyLife.value: Many live in city houses or villages; meals centre on cassava (foufou or chikwangue), fish, saka-saka leaves and plantains.

neighbours.value: Gabon, Cameroon, Central African Republic, DR Congo, Angola.

ideasReligions.value: Marxism–Leninism was the official ideology of the People’s Republic of the Congo (1969–91); Christianity is the main faith.

colonisation.value: A French colony (Middle Congo, part of French Equatorial Africa) until 1960; Brazzaville grew from Savorgnan de Brazza’s 1880 treaty with the Teke king Makoko.

riseSignals.value: Independence from France on 15 August 1960 under President Fulbert Youlou.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; oil booms in the late 1970s–80s and the 2000s brought high state revenues.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
